definition: Material science: by analyzing the chemical composition, physical properties, and inferred craftsmanship of materials, ancient craft techniques are reconstructed, reducing divine artifacts from myth to analyzable engineering materials.
core_case: The Diamond Snare is 'refined fine steel' (alloy steel), the Golden-Banded Staff is 'divine iron' (meteorite iron?), and the Palm-Leaf Fan is 'Great Yin leaf' (organic composite?). These materials correspond to real Ming Dynasty craft techniques.

artifact_material_reports.modern_equivalent: tungsten steel / high-speed steel (high hardness, wear- and corrosion-resistant)
crafting_process: Ore selection: collect iron, tungsten, and chromium ore
Steelmaking: blast-furnace smelting to remove impurities
Alloying: add tungsten and chromium to raise hardness
Quenching: oil- or water-quench to raise hardness
Tempering: low-temperature temper to reduce brittleness
artifact_material_reports.function_principle: Extremely hard; can collect any metal weapon (on metal impact the Diamond Snare does not deform while the weapon does)
artifact_material_reports.estimated_value: priceless · peak of Ming Dynasty craft
artifact_material_reports.archaeological_parallel: Han Dynasty hundred-refined steel + Tang Dynasty bintie steel · Ming Dynasty cloisonné technique

material_insights: Of the 8 artifacts, 5 are metal and 3 are composite, reflecting Ming Dynasty craft levels.
Meteorite iron / divine iron is the common 'mythical material,' corresponding to the Shang Dynasty tradition of using meteorite iron.
The Diamond Snare's 'fine steel' corresponds to Ming Dynasty hundred-refined steel; its hardness approaches diamond.
The Palm-Leaf Fan's 'Great Yin leaf' is the only plant-based composite, corresponding to Han Dynasty lacquerware.
The Golden Hoop Mantra is the only precious-metal artifact, reflecting Buddhism's tradition of valuing gold.
The material diversity reflects the Ming Dynasty's multifaceted craft: steel + ceramics + wood + precious metals + composites.
